title: I shipped a real-time 1v1 mobile strategy game (Unity + dedicated servers) built mostly with AI coding agents. What worked and what didn't
author: Pure-Championship371
selftext:
We just released RoyalCraft, a real-time 1v1 strategy game for Android and iOS. Think Clash Royale with an economy on top: you drag cards to summon units, but you also build gold mines, upgrade your castle and scout through fog of war. Three races, no gacha, no unit levels, no ads.

Most of the work was done with AI coding agents (mostly Claude Code), so here's an honest breakdown of where AI carried the project and where it needed a human watching closely.

Where AI did the heavy lifting

• Gameplay and netcode: Unity client plus server-authoritative dedicated servers on AWS GameLift (Seoul and US East). The agent wrote most of the systems: matchmaking, reconnects, fog of war that the server never leaks, ranked seasons.
• Audio: every sound effect and the music are synthesized from code with Python scripts. No sample packs, so there are no copyright worries for streamers.
• Localization: 14 languages. The AI translated everything and also built an in-editor tool that cycles every screen in every language and resolution and flags clipped or overlapping text.
• Live balance: all balance numbers live in a spreadsheet that gets pushed to the live servers without a rebuild. The agent runs simulations before a change goes out.
• Marketing assets: the trailer, App Store preview video and ad images come from an in-engine capture tool the agent wrote, plus Python compositing.

Where it went wrong

• Infra changes that "looked done": a server deploy silently dropped launch arguments, and we didn't notice for weeks. Now the rule is that nothing counts as done until it's verified in live logs.
• Mobile-only bugs: an iOS crash on match start turned out to be a font engine eating 2GB of memory. It never showed up in the editor, so the AI needed real device traces to find it.
• Text layout across languages: Thai tone marks overlapping, German strings overflowing. Translation was the easy part, fitting the text was the hard part.

My takeaway: AI is great at building and at grinding through boring breadth (14 languages, hundreds of sounds), but you have to be the one who insists on verification.

Happy to answer questions about the workflow.
